ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-31 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's quest for maritime access to the Red Sea is a critical issue that transcends mere economic considerations, becoming an existential matter for the nation. As the most populous landlocked country, Ethiopia's reliance on Djibouti for 95% of its trade exposes it to significant vulnerabilities, particularly given the militarization of the Red Sea and the geopolitical tensions in the region. The recent formation of alliances among Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia aims to isolate Ethiopia, further complicating its access to vital maritime routes. This situation is exacerbated by external military presences that threaten Ethiopia's sovereignty and economic stability. Ethiopia's demand for a reliable maritime corridor is not merely an expansionist ambition but a legitimate right essential for its survival and security. The international community, alongside regional organizations, must facilitate dialogue to address Ethiopia's concerns while ensuring the interests of neighboring states are respected, to prevent potential conflict and promote regional stability.

ethiopia.title: The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war - Al Majalla
ethiopia.content: The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war | Al Majalla ع Sections Politics Culture & Social Affairs Business & Economy Science & Technology Documents & Memoirs Regions Gulf MENA Europe USA Asia World More Videos Cartoons World in photos Infographics Profiles Newsletter LATEST ISSUE Magazine Archive النسخة العربية Politics Culture & Social Affairs Business & Economy Science & Technology The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war https://en.majalla.com/node/333885/politics/port-assab-and-risk-ethiopia-eritrea-war Politics The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Landlocked Ethiopia says sovereign access to the Red Sea is an ‘existential’ issue, and its troops are now massing on the border with its smaller neighbour, Eritrea. What next? Wikimedia Commons A false-color image of the area surrounding the coastal city of Assab and the Red Sea coast, based on satellite imagery data captured on 23 October 2019. The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. That dependence creates genuine economic vulnerabilities. Sign up for our Weekly Newsletter Get the best of Majalla, straight to your inbox. Your newsletter subscriptions are subject to Al Majalla privacy policy and terms and conditions . Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. ethiopia.summary: The port of Assab has become a focal point in the escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with Ethiopia asserting that access to the Red Sea is an "existential" issue. The historical context of the dispute dates back to colonial times, with Assab symbolizing Ethiopia's loss of direct maritime access following Eritrea's independence in 1993. Ethiopia's population and economy have grown significantly, increasing its need for diversified trade routes beyond its reliance on Djibouti. Recent developments, including Ethiopia's military buildup near the Eritrean border and the breakdown of diplomatic relations, have heightened fears of conflict. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has framed the issue as a historical grievance, while Eritrea views Assab as integral to its sovereignty. The situation is further complicated by regional dynamics, including foreign interests from countries like the UAE and Israel. The potential for war poses risks not only to the two nations but also to regional stability, particularly affecting Sudan amidst its ongoing civil conflict.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 28, 2026 (ENA)— Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced that the country has taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets and is set to receive four batteries of S-400 air defense systems. The Prime Minister described the move as a significant milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its national defense and security capabilities. In a social media post, PM Abiy said Ethiopia’s comprehensive efforts to sustainably ensure peace and security had reached a new milestone. He added that the growing readiness of the country’s defense forces was enhancing its ability to deter potential aggression. “Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” he said, adding that Ethiopia would also receive four S-400 air defense system batteries. Prime Minister Abiy expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the fighter jets a year ahead of the agreed schedule. He said the acquisition places Ethiopia at the forefront of Sub-Saharan African nations in equipping itself with the advanced fighter jets. The Prime Minister further elaborated that the development further strengthens Ethiopia’s sovereignty and enhances its defense capabilities, enabling the country to pursue its national security objectives while contributing to regional stability. The announcement comes as Prime Minister Abiy arrives in Moscow, Russia, to attend the Third Russia–Africa Summit, providing an opportunity to advance Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia and other African nations. The Prime Minister described the acquisition as a significant boost to Ethiopia’s collective security and its long-term efforts to safeguard national sovereignty and regional peace. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has received its first 12 Su-35 fighter jets and is set to acquire four S-400 air defense system batteries, as announced by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. This delivery marks a significant advancement in Ethiopia's national defense capabilities, aimed at enhancing security and deterring potential threats. In a social media statement, PM Abiy highlighted that this achievement is part of Ethiopia's broader strategy to ensure peace and security sustainably. He expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for expediting the delivery ahead of schedule. The acquisition positions Ethiopia as a leader in military modernization within Sub-Saharan Africa, reinforcing its sovereignty and defense capabilities. The announcement coincides with PM Abiy's visit to Moscow for the Third Russia–Africa Summit, which aims to strengthen Ethiopia's ties with Russia and other African nations. This development is seen as a crucial step in bolstering Ethiopia's collective security and long-term national objectives. (159 words)

EST to October 30, 2026, at 9:00 A.M. EST. To receive the Africa File, Ethiopia War Security Review, or Congo War Security Review via email, please subscribe here . Follow CTP on X , LinkedIn , and BlueSky for daily updates. Read CTP’s latest analysis on the war in Ethiopia in the weekly Africa File here . Key Takeaways: Northern Axis. The Ethiopian military has conducted consecutive days of drone strikes in Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF)-held Rama, a town on the Eritrean border, amid reported fighting around the Rama-Adwa highway. Western Axis. The Ethiopian military and TPLF continued clashing northwest of Shire as the ENDF attempts to consolidate control of the area. Central Axis. The Ethiopian military and the TDF have continued fighting over control of the mountainous Tigray interior. Northern Amhara Sector. The ENDF reportedly conducted drone strikes targeting the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) in mountainous areas around the A2 highway between Dessie and Woldia. Other Rebel Kinetic Activity. The Oromo Liberation Army reportedly clashed with federal and regional forces in western Oromia region. Major Domestic Political Developments. AFNM figure Eskinder Nega announced that he was leaving the AFNM. Regional and International Activity. Ethiopia and Russia reaffirmed their intent to strengthen ties at the Russia-Africa Summit, with Russia delivering fighter jets to Ethiopia amid the summit. Ethiopia welcomed the candidacy of Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh for United Nations-Secretary General. The Ethiopian Navy held a four-day forum on security in the Red Sea and conjoining waterways including naval officers from Djibouti, Oman, Puntland, Somaliland, and Yemen. Figure 1. ENDF and TPLF Battle Across Tigray Source: Michael DeAngelo, Liam Karr, and Alexander Brown Eastern Axis: Afar Region Nothing significant to report. Northern Axis: Rama-Zalambessa-Dallol The Ethiopian military (Ethiopian National Defense Force, ENDF) has conducted consecutive days of drone strikes in TPLF-held Rama, a town on the Eritrean border, amid reported fighting around the Rama-Adwa highway. The Tigray Defense Forces (TDF), the TPLF’s military wing, retook Rama on October 22 following an ENDF withdrawal from the town. [i] Several conflict trackers on social media have reported ENDF drone strikes in Rama the past few days, with the analyst and mapper The Ethiopian Conflict Map stating that the strikes began on October 27. [ii] The ENDF conducted a drone strike on October 30 that killed at least 12 civilians, who were reportedly collecting grain from a transport truck that had been struck the previous day. [iii] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and a pro-Fano account on X have reported fighting between the ENDF and TDF on both sides of highway that connects Rama to ENDF-held Adwa, which is approximately 20 miles to the south, since October 28. [iv] Western Axis: Humera-Addi Remets-Shire The ENDF and TDF continued clashing northwest of Shire as the ENDF attempts to consolidate control of the area. The two sides clashed near Adi Nebreid and Adi Hageray, which is 40 miles northwest of Shire, on October 27 and 28 after the ENDF reportedly advanced into the area. [v] Fighting reportedly occurred north of the two towns, which are on a road that connects Sheraro approximately 20 miles to the west. Pro-TPLF journalist Yonas Nigussie and a pro-Fano account on X separately reported that the TDF repelled the ENDF. [vi] Central Axis: Abiy Addi-Adwa-Axum Ethiopian federal forces and the TDF have continued fighting over control of the mountainous Tigray interior. Federal forces have continued efforts to clear the TDF from its mountain havens around Abiy Addi, which is 55 miles west of Mekele, after capturing both Abiy Addi and Zana on October 22. [vii] Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) and The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported that federal forces gained control of multiple areas around Kola Tembien, which is just northwest of Abiy Addi, amid clashes with the TDF from October 27 to 29. [viii] Federal forces have also attempted to clear the TDF from havens near Tigray’s city belt, specifically on both sides of Tigray’s main east-west highway. Federal forces have repeatedly clashed with the TDF around the highway since October 20. [ix] ACLED reported federal movements toward Werie Lehe, which is approximately 40 miles southeast of Adwa, from positions to the south and west on October 28. [x] The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported fighting between federal forces and the TDF in the area on the same day. [xi] Clashes also reportedly occurred near Chila, which is between Axum and Shire approximately 15 miles north of the east-west highway, on October 28 and 29 amid reported federal artillery strikes. [xii] Southern Axis: Mekele-Alamata-Sekota-Woldia Nothing significant to report. Northern Amhara Sector: From B22 Highway Northward The ENDF reportedly conducted drone strikes targeting the Amhara Fano National Movement in mountainous areas around the A2 highway between Dessie and Woldia. The Ethiopian Conflict Map and two pro-Fano sources reported on October 29 that the ENDF conducted strikes near Hayk, which is 20 miles north of Dessie. [xiii] The pro-Fano sources alleged that the strikes hit an internally displaced persons camp, killing over a dozen civilians. [xiv] Other Rebel Kinetic Activity The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) reportedly clashed with federal and regional forces in western Oromia region. Multiple news outlets had previously reported on October 20 and 21 that suspected OLA militants attacked a sugar factory in Fincha, which is in the Horo Guduru Welega zone approximately 175 miles northwest of Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital. [xv] The attack, which would have been one of the OLA’s first since the war between the federal government and Alliance for Survival rebel coalition began in September 2026, reportedly killed several security officers and elicited a federal drone strike against the militants. [xvi] The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported on October 29 that the OLA clashed again with federal police and Oromia regional forces in Fincha. [xvii] Major Domestic Political Developments AFNM figure Eskinder Nega announced that he was leaving the AFNM. Eskinder had led the Amhara Fano Peace Organization, one of the groups that merged to form the AFNM, and voiced support for AFNM’s creation in January 2026, despite reportedly declining to serve as its policy and strategy head. [xviii] Deutsche Welle reported on October 28 that Eskinder stated that he was leaving the AFNM due to the group’s membership in the Alliance for Survival, specifically citing the TPLF’s influence in the coalition. [xix] Regional and International Activity Ethiopia and Russia reaffirmed their intent to strengthen ties at the Russia-Africa Summit, with Russia delivering fighter jets to Ethiopia amid the summit. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on October 28 on the sidelines of the summit in Moscow and expressed their mutual interest in deepening cooperation between the two countries. [xx] Abiy emphasized nuclear energy cooperation as a priority, calling for increased funding and training for Ethiopian experts. [xxi] The Russian ambassador to Ethiopia said in an interview with Russian state media published on October 26 that Russia and Ethiopia are drafting an agreement to cooperate on the construction of a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia, with Abiy reporting progress on the agreement on October 29. [xxii] Russia delivered fighter jets to Ethiopia amid the summit as part of a preexisting deal. Abiy thanked Putin on X on October 28 for the delivery of Russian Su-35 fighter jets, which Abiy said Russia delivered a year ahead of schedule. [xxiii] Abiy stated that Russia would deliver 12 fighter jets, although the Russian state-owned arms exporter Rosoboronexport commented to Reuters that it had delivered two fighter jets to the Ethiopian Air Force. [xxiv] The prime minister also said that Russia will eventually deliver four S-400 surface-to-air missile batteries. [xxv] Abiy portrayed the delivery as part of Ethiopian efforts to “preemptively deter aggression.” [xxvi] Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel stated on X on October 28 that the delivery will support an Ethiopian “‘pre-emptive’ war of aggression.” [xxvii] Ethiopia welcomed the candidacy of Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh for United Nations-Secretary General. Nusseibeh previously announced her candidacy on October 22. [xxviii] The Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on X on October 29 that Ethiopia “welcomes” Nusseibeh’s candidacy, pointing to her diplomatic experience. [xxix] Nusseibeh expressed gratitude to the Ethiopian foreign ministry on October 30. [xxx] The Ethiopian Navy held a four-day forum on security in the Red Sea and conjoining waterways including naval officers from Djibouti, Oman, Puntland, Somaliland, and Yemen. The Ethiopian Navy hosted the forum, which was sponsored by the European Union, at its headquarters from October 26 to 29. [xxxi] The forum was intended to increase maritime cooperation among the participants in search-and-rescue operations and broader security matters. ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopia War Security Review for October 30, 2026, highlights ongoing military activities and clashes involving the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). The ENDF has conducted drone strikes in TPLF-held Rama, resulting in civilian casualties, while fighting continues around the Rama-Adwa highway. Clashes are reported northwest of Shire as the ENDF seeks to consolidate control in the region. In the mountainous Tigray interior, federal forces are engaged in combat with the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF). Additionally, the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) has faced drone strikes, allegedly hitting civilian areas. Political developments include the departure of AFNM figure Eskinder Nega, citing TPLF influence. Internationally, Ethiopia and Russia are strengthening ties, with Russia delivering fighter jets and discussing nuclear cooperation. Ethiopia also supports Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh's candidacy for UN Secretary-General and hosted a naval security forum with regional partners.

Password recovery Recover your password your email A password will be e-mailed to you. borkena Ethiopian News and Opinion Home Featured Latest News Business Opinion Video Amharic Entertainment Restaurant Travel Sport Books Blog Business Listings Jobs Support Us Contact Sign in / Join Sunday, November 1, 2026 Facebook Linkedin Telegram TikTok WhatsApp Instagram X Youtube Home Ethiopian News U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa Issues Security Alert Ethiopian News October 30, 2026 Updated: October 30, 2026 U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa Issues Security Alert October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Security situation remains volatile across Tigray, Afar, and Amhara as embassy warns citizens against travel File/SM Borkena Desk TORONTO, Canada — The United States Embassy in Addis Ababa has released an alert in a month regarding the security situation in the country. The latest alert seems to confirm that there is still fighting in the Tigray region of Ethiopia although the regional capital Mekelle is not experiencing active fighting. In an interview with Anchor Media on Thursday, the TPLF spokesperson Dr. Abraham Hagos stated that the organization has finalized preparation for counter-offensive and is reorganized for combat in five fronts. The statement from the Embassy on Wednesday this week stated “Fighting in Tigray appears to be concentrated in areas outside Mekelle and near the border with Eritrea.” It noted that Ethiopian Airlines flights to Shire and Axum, in the Tigray region remain suspended. As was the case with the travel advisory at the beginning of this month, the U.S. Embassy advised citizens to reconsider travelling to Ethiopia and avoid traveling to Afar, Amhara and Tigray regions of Ethiopia. It also advised citizens who are already in those areas to leave if safe to do so. Also, the embassy highlighted the security situation in Moyale, a border town between Ethiopia and Kenya where there had been intense conflict earlier this week. It stated that ” The embassy also continues to monitor ongoing fighting in Moyale, the primary border with Kenya, shared by both the Oromia and Somali regions, which appears to have calmed.” However, it warned that the situation “may change at any time.” Among the actions the embassy recommended to citizens is to avoid “military installations.” Earlier this month, the U.S. disclosed military attacks targeting the capital Addis Ababa as local sources were reporting a drone attack targeting Defense Force Headquarters in the capital Addis Ababa – which Ethiopia did not confirm. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio linked the attacks to what he described as “separatists.” Notably, seven armed groups operating in the different parts of the country formed a coalition in September. It was within less than three weeks after the announcement of the coalition that the Ethiopian Defense Force launched its military operation in the Tigray region. Tigray People’s Liberation Front ( TPLF ) fighters withdrew from many towns in the region including Mekelle which they describe as “strategic retreat” However, media outlets affiliated with the government claim that the TPLF was militarily defeated and is now waging a guerilla war across Northern Tigray. On Friday, Samora Yenus, former defense chief and TPLF member, stated that the TPLF was defeated. He added “Guerilla war is no longer viable in the Tigray region.” __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Ethiopian Sports News Join the conversation. ethiopia.summary: The U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa has issued a security alert regarding the ongoing volatile situation in Ethiopia, particularly in the Tigray, Afar, and Amhara regions. The alert indicates that while the regional capital, Mekelle, is not currently experiencing active fighting, clashes continue in surrounding areas, especially near the Eritrean border. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) has announced preparations for a counter-offensive, suggesting a potential escalation in conflict. The embassy has advised American citizens to reconsider travel to Ethiopia and to avoid the aforementioned regions, urging those already there to leave if safe. Additionally, the embassy is monitoring tensions in Moyale, a border town with Kenya, where recent conflicts have occurred. The situation remains fluid, with warnings to avoid military installations and acknowledgment of recent drone attacks in Addis Ababa, which have not been officially confirmed by Ethiopian authorities.

somalia.summary: The United Nations has officially concluded over 30 years of direct political engagement in Somalia, marking a significant transition in its involvement in the country. This decision follows a two-year transition period for its political mission, which aimed to support Somalia in strengthening its political institutions, governance, and security. The end of this political mission signifies a shift in the UN's approach, moving away from direct political involvement while still maintaining a presence in the region. Although the political engagement has ceased, the UN will continue its various activities in Somalia, indicating that its commitment to the country's development and stability remains intact. This transition reflects the evolving dynamics in Somalia as it seeks to build a more resilient political framework.

somalia.title: WHERE ARE THE SOMALI INTELLECTUALS WHO WILL STAND UP TO SAVE SOMALIA? - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: WHERE ARE THE SOMALI INTELLECTUALS WHO WILL STAND UP TO SAVE SOMALIA? - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION WHERE ARE THE SOMALI INTELLECTUALS WHO WILL STAND UP TO SAVE SOMALIA? Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Amb. Ali Mohamed Mohamud Cagabarur Saturday October 31, 2026 Lessons from 1990, the Responsibility of Today’s Intellectuals, and the Dangers of Silence at Critical Moments in a Nation’s History History is not merely a record of events that nations have experienced. It also carries lessons and warnings from which every generation must learn. A nation that fails to learn from the mistakes of its past risks confronting the same tragedies again. Somalia is a clear example of a country where the collapse of state institutions left political, social, and economic wounds from which the nation has yet to fully recover. The collapse of the central government in 1991 was not simply the end of a political system. It triggered institutional breakdown, civil war, mass displacement, and national fragmentation, the consequences of which have affected generations. Today, after decades of efforts to rebuild state institutions, Somalia is once again experiencing political disputes, constitutional disagreements, and growing mistrust among political stakeholders. Although the circumstances today differ significantly from those of 1990, history reminds us of the importance of resolving political differences before they escalate into a national crisis. This raises a question that deserves serious reflection: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up to defend statehood, speak truth to those in power, unite the people, and prevent threats that could undermine the nation’s future? The Lesson of 1990: When Intellectuals Warned of National Collapse In late 1990, as Somalia moved closer to political and security turmoil, a group of prominent Somali intellectuals and respected national figures emerged. They included former politicians, academics, religious scholars, traditional elders, and individuals who commanded considerable respect within society. This group, widely known as the Manifesto Group, sought to play a role in preventing the impending collapse of the Somali state. They called for political reform, dialogue, and a peaceful resolution to the escalating national crisis. The historical significance of their initiative was not limited to the statement they issued. More importantly, it reflected their conviction that intellectual leadership was not merely a matter of titles, prestige, or social recognition. Rather, it carried a patriotic responsibility to speak out when the future of the nation was at risk. Although their efforts ultimately failed to prevent the collapse of the central government in 1991, they left an important historical lesson: individuals possessing knowledge, experience, and social influence have a responsibility to warn of impending dangers, facilitate dialogue, and seek solutions during periods of national crisis. The collapse of 1991 demonstrated that once public confidence, state institutions, and political leadership have been severely undermined, rebuilding them can take decades. The question facing Somalia today is therefore not merely why the state collapsed in 1991, but what lessons we have learned from that experience and what measures we are taking to prevent the repetition of past mistakes. Somalia Today: Political Disputes and the Responsibility of Intellectuals Somalia today is not Somalia of 1990. The country has government institutions, a federal political system, a constitution, and ongoing efforts to strengthen statehood. Nevertheless, the existence of these institutions alone does not guarantee political stability without public trust, accountability, and a shared national understanding of the country's future direction. Constitutional disputes, disagreements between the Federal Government and certain Federal Member States, and differing positions on the electoral process demonstrate the need for inclusive political dialogue. Statehood is not sustained by institutional authority alone. It depends on legitimacy, public confidence, respect for the constitution, and the ability of political leaders to manage disagreements while safeguarding the national interest. When political disagreements are treated as battles in which one side must defeat the other, rather than as issues requiring dialogue and compromise, achieving sustainable solutions becomes increasingly difficult. This is precisely where the responsibility of Somali intellectuals begins. Every society has individuals who may not hold public office but possess knowledge, experience, credibility, and the ability to influence public opinion and political decision-making. Such individuals can serve as bridges between opposing parties, independent voices willing to speak the truth, and constructive forces working to protect the national interest. However, they cannot fulfill this responsibility if they become absorbed in political rivalries, align themselves with competing factions, or remain silent on matters of national importance to protect personal relationships and private interests. True intellectual leadership does not mean agreeing with everything those in power do. It means having the courage to tell them the truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable or unwelcome. The Silence of Intellectuals: A Responsibility That Cannot Be Evaded There is a fundamental difference between neutrality and silence. Neutrality means remaining independent of competing political interests and assessing events according to fairness, evidence, and conscience. Silence, however, when motivated by fear, personal interests, or a desire to please those in power, can amount to an abandonment of one's responsibility to society. Somali intellectuals must be able to engage equally with government leaders, opposition figures, and all political stakeholders. They must speak openly about political mistakes without directing criticism exclusively at one side or defending those with whom they share personal or political interests. Religious scholars, academics, former political leaders, diplomats, businesspeople, traditional elders, women, and young Somalis all share a responsibility to protect social cohesion and the continuity of Somali statehood. Former political leaders and experienced diplomats, in particular, should draw upon the lessons they have learned from leadership, political negotiations, and conflict resolution. Their experience should serve the national interest rather than being confined to commentary and observation. Somalia does not need intellectuals who automatically align themselves with those currently in power or those seeking to replace them. It needs independent national voices whose commitment to the country transcends temporary political interests. A nation cannot be saved through applause and unquestioning praise. It is safeguarded through sincere advice, truthfulness, national unity, and leadership that accepts accountability. The Urgent Need for a National Gathering One of the most important lessons from the efforts of Somali intellectuals in 1990 is that political disputes should not be allowed to deteriorate to the point where peaceful resolution becomes increasingly difficult. Somali intellectuals should initiate independent national consultations to address the country's political situation, constitutional disagreements, electoral processes, and the restoration of confidence in national institutions. Such consultations should remain independent of the Federal Government, Federal Member States, and opposition groups. They should bring together respected individuals known for their integrity, knowledge, impartiality, and experience. The objective should not be to establish another political organization or create a competing center of authority. Rather, it should be to develop a unified civic voice, formulate practical recommendations, and facilitate mediation among political stakeholders. Intellectuals should encourage all parties to resolve constitutional disputes through lawful procedures and dialogue, pursue an electoral process grounded in broad political agreement, and ensure that public authority is exercised in the national interest. Equally important is the need to warn against the exploitation of clan divisions, public incitement, and inflammatory political rhetoric that could intensify tensions. A country that has endured decades of civil conflict and fragmentation needs political leadership willing to compromise and a society capable of preventing political disagreements from escalating into violence. Government and Opposition: A Shared National Responsibility The responsibility to protect Somali statehood does not rest exclusively with those currently in office, nor does it belong solely to the opposition. It is a shared obligation among political stakeholders and society as a whole. Every government has a duty to uphold the constitution, strengthen national institutions, protect citizens' rights, and resolve political disagreements through dialogue and mutual understanding. Similarly, the opposition has a responsibility to present constructive political alternatives, preserve peace, and avoid actions that could undermine the continuity of state institutions. Political disagreement is a natural and legitimate feature of democracy. What matters is ensuring that such disagreements do not destroy the institutions and constitutional principles within which all political actors must operate. Those who hold public office today must recognize that political authority is temporary, while statehood is a national inheritance belonging to both present and future generations. The Somali state must always be greater than the individual who leads it, the political party that governs it, or any group seeking to control it. Conclusion: Let Us Not Become Silent Spectators Whom History Will Hold Accountable Somalia has paid an extraordinarily high price for the collapse of its state institutions. Thousands of families lost loved ones, while millions of Somalis experienced displacement, exile, and hardship as a result of civil conflict and institutional breakdown. Generations of Somalis have grown up without adequate public services, reliable security, or sufficient economic opportunities to build their futures. Today, our generation carries a historic responsibility to protect what has been rebuilt and prevent mistakes that could undermine decades of state-building efforts. The intellectuals of 1990 attempted to warn the nation of the dangers it faced. Today, more than fourteen years after the establishment of the non-transitional Federal Government in 2012, a critical question must be asked: Who will assume the responsibility of bringing national voices together, reducing political tensions, and safeguarding the future of Somali statehood? The time has come for Somali intellectuals to move beyond isolated statements, media commentary, and political alignments toward meaningful consultations and a collective effort to identify national solutions. History remembers more than the leaders who held political power. It also remembers those who demonstrated the courage to defend the public interest, those who worked to prevent national tragedies, and those who remained silent when their country needed them most. Somali statehood is a national inheritance achieved through decades of struggle and immense sacrifice. It is not the property of any particular government, political party, or group in power. It is a collective responsibility belonging to the entire Somali people. The question, therefore, remains: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up today to safeguard Somalia's future? Somalia must not wait for another national catastrophe to recognize the value of statehood. What the country needs is an awakened national conscience, leadership willing to accept constructive advice, and intellectuals with the courage to speak the truth. A nation must be saved while there is still an opportunity to correct its course—not after its collapse has become an irreversible reality. Writer: Amb. It reflects on the collapse of Somalia's state institutions in 1991, which led to civil war and national fragmentation. The author, Amb. Ali Mohamed Mohamud Cagabarur, argues that today's intellectuals must take responsibility to prevent history from repeating itself. While Somalia has made strides in establishing government institutions, political disputes and a lack of public trust threaten stability. Intellectuals are called upon to facilitate dialogue, promote national unity, and engage with all political stakeholders without aligning with specific factions. The article stresses that true leadership involves speaking uncomfortable truths and fostering a collective civic voice to address constitutional disagreements and electoral processes. somalia.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly 20 years - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly 20 years - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly 20 years 12 Shares Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Friday October 30, 2026 Kampala (HOL) — Uganda has begun withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military deployments, its army chief announced Thursday, marking the start of a security handover to Somali forces as the African Union mission faces mounting financial and political pressure. “As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defense forces, wrote on X. advertisements Ugandan authorities have not publicly announced how many troops are leaving, which bases will be handed over first or when the withdrawal will be completed. Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM. The African Union authorized 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the start of 2025. AUSSOM’s mandate includes supporting Somali forces against al-Shabab, protecting civilians and key infrastructure, and gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somali security institutions. The mission’s current transition plan envisages a phased drawdown toward a final exit by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent in the African Union Mission in Somalia, or AMISOM, becoming one of the longest-serving foreign military contributors to the country’s security operations. Ugandan forces have since fought in some of the most significant battles against al-Shabab and have operated across Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has also come at a heavy cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in al-Shabab attacks, including major assaults on African Union bases over the course of the mission. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces persistent funding shortages. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable financing threatens the mission’s operations and has called for additional international support. The AU has also emphasized that decisions over AUSSOM’s future and troop withdrawals should be based on assessments of conditions on the ground and coordinated with Somalia to avoid creating security gaps. Uganda has remained a central part of that security architecture. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to control or operate across parts of rural southern and central Somalia despite nearly two decades of military pressure from Somali forces and their international partners. Kainerugaba’s announcement therefore represents a significant shift in Uganda’s long-running role in Somalia, but it remains unclear whether the move marks the beginning of a full national withdrawal or a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the chief of Uganda’s defense forces. This move marks the beginning of a security transition to Somali forces amid increasing financial and political pressures on the African Union mission, known as AUSSOM. Although the exact number of troops being withdrawn and the timeline for completion remain undisclosed, Uganda has been the largest contributor to AUSSOM, which was established to support Somali forces against the militant group al-Shabab. The mission aims to gradually transfer security responsibilities to Somali institutions, with a planned phased drawdown by December 2029, contingent on security conditions. Uganda's involvement has been significant, with troops engaged in key battles and suffering casualties. The withdrawal raises questions about the future of security in Somalia, especially given the ongoing threat from al-Shabab and the mission's funding challenges.

The Maritime Security Centre–Indian Ocean (MSCIO), which supports the EU's Operation ATALANTA, said the Iranian fishing vessel Azini was reportedly hijacked at approximately 09:00 UTC on October 29. In an update displayed on October 31, MSCIO said the vessel was approaching a maritime traffic lane and could potentially be used as a mothership to support additional piracy operations. The warning does not establish that the Azini has been used to launch attacks. The safety of its crew remains unknown, and authorities have not identified those responsible for the reported hijacking. The vessel's reported movement toward a shipping traffic lane has raised concerns about possible threats to merchant ships operating off Somalia's northeastern coast. A fishing vessel used as a pirate mothership could serve as a base for attacks beyond the immediate location of the original incident, potentially exposing other vessels to additional security risks. MSCIO has not reported any confirmed attacks launched from the Azini. Shipping Operators Urged to Remain Vigilant MSCIO urged vessels operating near the reported incident to maintain heightened vigilance, follow maritime security guidance and report suspicious activity. The advisory comes as Operation ATALANTA investigates the circumstances surrounding the reported seizure. For commercial shipping operators, the immediate concern is whether the incident remains isolated or develops into a wider threat along nearby maritime routes. The potential use of the Azini as a mothership is central to the warning, although authorities have not established that the vessel is being used for piracy operations. No confirmed follow-on attacks have been identified in MSCIO's notice. advertisements Incident Reported Off Puntland Coast Puntland Post, a regional news outlet, separately reported that the incident occurred off Banderbayla on Somalia's northeastern coast. The publication also reported that two Somali guards were among those aboard the Iranian vessel. Neither detail has been independently verified, and Puntland Post did not identify the sources behind its account. MSCIO has not provided a verified account from the crew or established who carried out the reported hijacking. The available information leaves the vessel's current status, the condition of those aboard and the identity of the suspected attackers unresolved. Investigation Focuses on Potential Piracy Threat Operation ATALANTA is investigating the reported incident as maritime authorities continue to warn nearby vessels of a possible security threat. The MSCIO advisory does not establish the circumstances of the initial boarding or confirm whether the vessel is currently under the control of suspected pirates. For commercial ship operators, the next critical development will be whether authorities can establish the Azini's status and determine if the vessel poses an active threat to nearby shipping. Until then, MSCIO's guidance remains focused on heightened vigilance and reporting suspicious activity, with the risk of further pirate attacks still unconfirmed. somalia.content: Somalia Faces Rising Rift Valley Fever Risk, Threatening Livestock Livelihoods - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Faces Rising Rift Valley Fever Risk, Threatening Livestock Livelihoods Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday October 31, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia faces a growing risk of Rift Valley fever that could threaten livestock-dependent livelihoods, after the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the regional bloc IGAD identified the country among six facing the highest assessed risk of the disease. The warning, issued on October 30, comes as El Niño-related rainfall creates favourable conditions for the spread of the mosquito-borne virus across Eastern Africa. FAO's October assessment identified newly suitable areas for transmission in southern Somalia and forecast a further expansion of favourable conditions across the region through January 2027. The assessment does not confirm an outbreak in Somalia. Instead, it signals an increased risk that authorities must prepare for before infections emerge or spread. The threat carries economic implications for communities that depend on livestock for their livelihoods. Rift Valley fever can cause severe illness in animals and humans, while livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can inflict significant financial damage on affected households. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the disease can cause serious illness in livestock, threatening the animals on which many rural livelihoods depend. For livestock owners, the potential losses extend beyond animals that die from infection. Pregnancy losses can also undermine the productive capacity of affected herds, increasing the economic burden of the disease. Rainfall Raises Transmission Risk Heavy rainfall is a central factor behind the latest warning. Wet conditions can expand mosquito breeding grounds, increasing the potential for transmission. Movements of livestock can also contribute to the spread of infection, making surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries important. The FAO assessment indicates that environmental conditions suitable for transmission have emerged in additional areas of southern Somalia. It also forecasts that conditions favourable to the disease could expand across Eastern Africa through January 2027, extending the period during which authorities may need to maintain heightened surveillance. The warning places Somalia within a broader regional risk picture rather than identifying a confirmed national outbreak. Agencies Call for Early Action FAO and IGAD urged countries facing elevated risk to strengthen targeted surveillance, position vaccines and essential supplies in advance, and coordinate animal-health and public-health responses across borders. The recommended measures are intended to improve preparedness before outbreaks place additional pressure on livestock owners and health services. Cross-border coordination is particularly important because livestock movements can contribute to disease transmission, while rainfall-driven mosquito breeding conditions may affect multiple countries. The agencies' recommendations focus on detecting potential infections and ensuring that essential resources are available when needed. advertisements Human Health and Livestock Losses Rift Valley fever poses a dual threat to animal production and human health. The WHO says most human infections occur through contact with the blood or organs of infected animals. People can also become infected through bites from mosquitoes carrying the virus. No human-to-human transmission has been documented, according to the WHO. The disease's impact on animals is a major economic concern. Livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can reduce the productive value of affected herds and threaten the livelihoods of households that rely on them. Somalia has experienced Rift Valley fever during earlier periods of exceptional rainfall. The WHO records a major outbreak in 1997–98 that affected Somalia, Kenya and Tanzania following an El Niño event accompanied by extensive flooding. That history provides a precedent for the current concern, although the latest assessment identifies transmission risk rather than confirmed infections. For Somalia, the immediate priority is preparedness. The effectiveness of targeted surveillance, advance positioning of vaccines and supplies, and coordination with neighbouring countries will be critical as rainfall-related transmission conditions are forecast to persist through January 2027. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the regional bloc IGAD have identified Somalia among six countries at high risk due to favorable conditions for the disease's spread, exacerbated by El Niño-related rainfall. Although no outbreak has been confirmed, the FAO's assessment warns of newly suitable transmission areas in southern Somalia and predicts that these conditions may persist through January 2027. The decision was announced in an official notice published in the U.S. Federal Register on October 27, 2026, following a Coast Guard assessment of security arrangements at Somalia's ports. advertisements The Coast Guard determined that Somalia is not currently maintaining effective measures to prevent acts of terrorism at its port facilities. As a result, vessels arriving in the United States from Somali ports will be subject to additional security and port entry requirements. The measures were introduced under powers granted by the Maritime Transportation Security Act and other federal laws governing maritime and port security. Somalia is now among 24 countries identified by the United States as failing to maintain effective counterterrorism measures at their ports. Others on the list include Iran, Iraq, Libya, Sudan, Syria, Yemen, Venezuela and North Korea. According to the Federal Register notice, the decision took effect on October 27, 2026. The notice was signed by Admiral Nathan A. Moore, the Coast Guard's Deputy Commandant for Operations. The designation means vessels arriving from Somali ports will face additional security procedures when entering U.S. waters. However, the notice does not detail all the specific measures that affected vessels will be required to follow. More News WHERE ARE THE SOMALI INTELLECTUALS WHO WILL STAND UP TO SAVE SOMALIA? Amb. somalia.content: UN political mission in Somalia closes after more than three decades - TRT Afrika | English | English POLITICS AFRICA TÜRKİYE OPINION FEATURES SPORTS AFRICA 2 min read UN political mission in Somalia closes after more than three decades The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia formally ended its operations on Saturday, concluding more than three decades of UN political engagement in the Horn of Africa country. Share Somalia had requested an end to UN's longstanding political mission in the country. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia formally ended its operations on Saturday, concluding a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN political engagement in the Horn of Africa country. The closure of the mission, known as UNTMIS, came at the request of the Somali government, according to a statement issued by the mission. The UN said successive political missions had supported Somalia through critical stages of peacebuilding and state-building, helping Somali-led efforts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and promote national reconciliation. "Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia — rather, it marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another," said Raisedon Zenenga, the mission's officer-in-charge and deputy special representative of the UN secretary-general for Somalia. UN says it is still committed to long-lasting peace efforts in Somalia The UN said it would remain committed to Somalia through its resident agencies and broader presence in the country, supporting efforts toward peace, stability, sustainable development and prosperity. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres commended the determination and resilience of the Somali people despite the challenges facing the country. "I call for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions and protect human rights," Guterres said on X social network. Series of UN political missions in Somalia The closure marks the end of a series of UN political missions in Somalia that began with the establishment of the UN Political Office for Somalia in 1995. The office was succeeded by the UN Assistance Mission in Somalia in 2013, which continued supporting the country's political and institutional development. In 2024, the UN launched the Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, beginning the final phase of the international body's political mission presence in the country. The milestone follows a structured two-year transition process, culminating in the handover of governance responsibilities to federal Somali institutions. In an official statement, Acting Mission Head and Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Somalia, Raisedon Zenenga, emphasized that the closure does not mark an end to UN-Somalia cooperation, but rather opens a new chapter of bilateral partnership.
